title: Permit Map
user: Engineers using coding agents across several repositories who need to see the effective allow/deny policy before an agent runs.

evidence.quote_or_summary: An Ask HN poster directly asks how teams provide AI agents access to credentials and secrets.
A 26-reaction Claude Code issue reports that a project permissions block replaces global permissions, forcing duplicated settings and surprising prompts.

recurrence: Two independent 2026 reports across HN and a coding-agent tracker; policy ambiguity is a security and productivity problem whenever repos add local rules.
current_workaround: Hand-read several JSON settings files, duplicate global rules into projects, and discover mismatches through prompts or failed tool calls.
incumbents_and_gap: Claude Code and Codex expose their own settings, while secret managers store values; neither supplies a vendor-neutral, resolved policy view across global, repo, and worktree layers.
smallest_useful_product: A local CLI that reads configured agent policy files, resolves precedence into an allow/deny table, highlights shadowed rules, and emits a reviewable Markdown report. Non-goals: running agents, storing secrets, or changing vendor settings.
success_measure: In a pilot, 80% of users identify at least one unexpected effective permission before an agent session, with zero credentials read by the tool.
monetization: free — trustworthy policy inspection benefits from open adapters and local operation.
constraints: Parse only local configuration; never read secret values; adapters must clearly state unsupported precedence semantics.
why_distinct: It is a resolved-policy inspector, not another agent, secret vault, or permission system.

title: Worktree Secret Broker
user: Developers creating disposable coding-agent worktrees who need a tested, least-privilege way to make only required development secrets available.

evidence.quote_or_summary: An Ask HN thread asks for best practices preventing credentials and secrets from being committed while agentic building is common.
A Codex App request says new worktrees need selected .env and .npmrc secrets and asks for a safe carry-over mechanism.

recurrence: Two 2026 worktree/agent users describe the same boundary: code needs configuration, but copying files risks committing or overexposing it.
current_workaround: Copy .env files manually, use symlinks, paste values into shells, or broadly expose a developer's secret-manager session.
incumbents_and_gap: 1Password, Doppler, direnv, and vendor worktrees manage pieces of the workflow; none produces a short-lived per-worktree secret lease with an explicit audit of requested variable names.
smallest_useful_product: A local CLI that maps approved variable names to OS-keychain/1Password references, injects them into one named worktree process, and prints an expiry/revocation receipt. Non-goals: cloud vault hosting, secret scanning, or sharing production credentials.
success_measure: At least 90% of pilot worktrees start without copying a secret file, and no broker-managed value appears in git diff or process history tests.
monetization: one-time — the value is a local safety utility, not a new secret-management subscription.
constraints: Use OS keychains or existing vault CLIs; never persist plaintext; default-deny production-labelled secrets; document shell/process-environment exposure limits.
why_distinct: It brokers temporary worktree access rather than replacing an organization's secret manager.

title: Boundary Replay
user: Backend engineers diagnosing production failures across queues, webhooks, and third-party APIs who need a scrubbed reproduction at the service boundary.

evidence.quote_or_summary: An Ask HN developer asks how teams debug production failures across internal services, Stripe/Twilio, queues, and webhooks.
Sentry tracks demand to capture network request and response bodies in Mobile Replay, showing that stack traces alone omit the failing boundary.

recurrence: Production investigation and network-body capture are requested in separate communities; failures at integrations are difficult to reproduce from logs alone.
current_workaround: Correlate traces and logs manually, copy sanitized curl commands into tickets, or retry against production-adjacent systems.
incumbents_and_gap: Sentry, Datadog, and OpenTelemetry preserve observability signals; they do not turn a selected cross-service boundary into a local, redactable replay fixture with causality notes.
smallest_useful_product: A sidecar/CLI that captures opted-in HTTP or webhook exchanges, applies field-level redaction, pairs them with trace IDs, and exports a runnable local mock fixture. Non-goals: traffic interception by default, production replay, or a tracing backend.
success_measure: For seeded integration failures, a team reproduces 70% using an exported bundle without accessing the original production system.
monetization: freemium — an open local exporter earns trust; paid team redaction policy packs can follow.
constraints: Explicit opt-in capture only; secrets/PII redaction before disk write; signed webhooks must be re-signed for mock use; no production target replay.
why_distinct: The artifact is a safe reproduction bundle at an integration boundary, not another APM dashboard.

title: Drain Check
user: Small platform teams adding managed log drains who need to know a drain's volume, fields, and privacy risk before turning it on continuously.

evidence.quote_or_summary: An Ask HN poster says debugging requires manually inspecting production alongside logs and asks how often others do the same.
A 39-reaction Sentry issue requests Heroku Log Drain support and asks interested users for their use cases.

recurrence: The HN investigation workflow and a high-interest log-drain request show that log routing is expanding, while teams still need to validate what arrives.
current_workaround: Enable a drain, inspect a vendor UI after the fact, estimate costs from provider docs, and manually discover sensitive fields.
incumbents_and_gap: Sentry, Better Stack, and Datadog ingest logs, but they are destinations; a short preflight that samples a drain and makes its data contract reviewable is missing.
smallest_useful_product: A local receiver that accepts a 10-minute drain sample, reports event rate/field types/likely secrets, and generates a forwarding configuration plus retention estimate. Non-goals: long-term log storage, alerting, or log search.
success_measure: A pilot identifies 95% of configured sensitive-field patterns before forwarding production logs, and estimates event volume within 25% after one day.
monetization: free — preflight transparency should not require sending logs to a new vendor.
constraints: Bind locally by default; discard bodies after aggregation unless explicitly saved; ship conservative secret detectors and clear false-positive handling.
why_distinct: It validates a logging connection before commitment instead of competing as a log destination.

title: Legacy Change Radar
user: Maintainers reviewing agent-authored changes in large established applications who need to find changed dependency and risk surfaces before line-by-line review.

evidence.quote_or_summary: An Ask HN poster asks how to harden agentic changes to a 15-year-old, 1M+ line SaaS before review.
A 226-reaction Codex request wants IDE-integrated red/green diffs and approval rather than terminal-only change review.

recurrence: One large-codebase safety request and strong demand for better change approval point to review context, not code generation, as the bottleneck.
current_workaround: Read raw diffs, run broad CI, ask the author for context, and discover touched configuration or generated artifacts late.
incumbents_and_gap: GitHub/GitLab review and IDE diff views show changed lines; CodeQL and CI run checks. They do not summarize blast radius across ownership, migrations, public APIs, and configuration as a compact review appendix.
smallest_useful_product: A CI CLI that turns a git diff into a Markdown risk card: affected owners, dependency edges, config/migration/API markers, and required named checks. Non-goals: code generation, autonomous approval, or replacing existing CI.
success_measure: In 30 pilot pull requests, reviewers identify a relevant non-line-level risk in at least 20% and do not increase median review time by more than five minutes.
monetization: freemium — local analysis can be open; hosted policy/ownership integrations are team value.
constraints: Run repository-local; explain every inferred edge; never claim a risk score proves correctness; support language adapters incrementally.
why_distinct: It creates a reviewable blast-radius artifact rather than another AI reviewer or diff viewer.

title: Change Checkpoints
user: Teams accepting rapid agent or developer edits who need a durable checkpoint tying a workspace state, tests, and rollback instructions together.

evidence.quote_or_summary: An Ask HN thread asks whether a stronger process is needed to vet automated code because quality signals have become harder to trust.
A 206-reaction Codex request asks for one rewind checkpoint that restores both chat context and applied workspace edits.

recurrence: The discussion of stronger vetting and high-interest checkpoint restoration both reflect that reverting code without its validation context is insufficient.
current_workaround: Use git commits/stashes, CI links, screenshots, and chat transcripts that are disconnected from one another.
incumbents_and_gap: Git provides commits and Codex offers session checkpoints; neither makes a portable, tool-independent checkpoint manifest containing exact diff, commands, environment assertions, and rollback note.
smallest_useful_product: A CLI that records a named checkpoint from git state, selected commands and their exit status, then writes a signed JSON/Markdown manifest with a verified restore command. Non-goals: source hosting, chat retention, or automatic rollback in production.
success_measure: At least 90% of sampled checkpoints reproduce their recorded git state and validation command results on a clean clone.
monetization: one-time — it is a local engineering control with episodic team rollout value.
constraints: Never embed secrets or command output by default; hash artifacts; clearly mark non-reproducible environment-dependent commands.
why_distinct: It makes validation context portable across agents and editors instead of offering yet another undo button.

title: Result Envelope
user: MCP and CLI tool authors who need to return large structured results to models without silently truncating, over-tokenizing, or hiding the useful rows.

evidence.quote_or_summary: An Ask HN poster asks what format lets a tool report tabular or structured data effectively to an LLM.
A 39-reaction MCP issue says tool results currently must complete in full before anything returns to the client, limiting large or slow results.

recurrence: The current HN format question and the MCP streaming request identify a practical protocol gap at the tool-result boundary.
current_workaround: Dump JSON/CSV into a prompt, hand-write summaries, paginate ad hoc, or make the model issue repeated query calls.
incumbents_and_gap: MCP transports tool content and data libraries serialize formats, but neither gives tool authors a deterministic, token-budgeted result envelope with a stable drill-down contract.
smallest_useful_product: An npm library and CLI that turns rows/JSON into a manifest, compact summary, schema, stable page cursors, and optional streamed chunks; it includes a local inspector. Non-goals: model calls, RAG, or database hosting.
success_measure: On a benchmark of 20 tabular tool responses, users retrieve a target value in one or two tool calls while using at least 50% fewer result tokens than raw JSON.
monetization: free — interoperability requires a broadly adopted open format and reference implementation.
constraints: Do not claim universal model optimization; preserve types and provenance; enforce configurable row and byte caps; avoid embedding sensitive sample rows in telemetry.
why_distinct: It is transport/representation infrastructure, not a thin LLM summary wrapper.

title: Action Parity Probe
user: Teams evaluating local or alternate runners after GitHub Actions incidents who need evidence of workflow behavior differences before moving CI.

evidence.quote_or_summary: An Ask HN thread asks for alternatives to GitHub Actions after outages, noting that even external runners still depend on GitHub triggers.
A 40-reaction act issue documents a command available on GitHub-hosted runners but absent locally, illustrating runner-environment drift.

recurrence: Reliance on Actions triggers and runner parity are separate recurring constraints; a migration fails when a workflow only works in one environment.
current_workaround: Run act locally, read image documentation, fix failures one by one, and only discover platform differences after an outage or cutover.
incumbents_and_gap: act, GitHub Actions, and CI vendors execute workflows; none produces a focused compatibility report comparing declared workflow requirements against a chosen runner profile.
smallest_useful_product: A CLI that statically inventories workflow actions, images, permissions, service containers, and shell assumptions, then runs a small probe suite and emits a portable/nonportable report. Non-goals: a CI runner, workflow translation, or hosted execution.
success_measure: For ten known cross-runner failures, the probe flags at least eight before a full migration run.
monetization: free — portability checks must be neutral across CI vendors.
constraints: Never execute untrusted workflows without explicit sandbox mode; keep vendor profiles versioned; distinguish static warnings from observed failures.
why_distinct: It measures migration readiness rather than becoming another GitHub Actions substitute.

title: GitHub Exit Inventory
user: Small software teams considering a GitHub fallback who need to know which repository, CI, OAuth, release, and integration dependencies make a move costly.

evidence.quote_or_summary: An Ask HN poster asks why a small team needs GitHub once repositories, CI/CD, PRs, packages, and integrations are wired into it.
A 57-reaction Sentry request for Gitea/Gogs support explicitly seeks parity with existing GitLab/GitHub integrations.

recurrence: The current lock-in question and the established demand for forge integration parity show that repository migration is an integration inventory problem, not only git export.
current_workaround: Clone repositories, list Actions and apps manually, search documentation, and learn missing integrations during a migration.
incumbents_and_gap: GitHub's export APIs and Gitea/GitLab importers move pieces of data; they do not provide a local, evidence-backed dependency map of what breaks or needs replacement.
smallest_useful_product: A read-only CLI that inventories repositories, Actions, webhooks, GitHub Apps/OAuth references, packages, branch rules, and issue links, then writes a migration checklist with alternatives marked as verified or unknown. Non-goals: executing migration, mirroring private code, or hosting git.
success_measure: A team produces a complete dependency inventory in under 30 minutes and finds no unlisted GitHub dependency during a planned dry run.
monetization: one-time — migration planning is episodic and users seeking portability should not acquire a recurring platform fee.
constraints: Use minimum read-only API scopes; do not upload repository metadata; product names must not imply compatibility guarantees; respect GitHub rate limits.
why_distinct: It helps teams quantify and plan portability without cloning GitHub or another forge.

title: Restore Drill
user: Teams relying on managed Postgres backups who need to prove that a recent backup restores into their intended version and extension set before an outage.

evidence.quote_or_summary: An Ask HN report describes a production Supabase database remaining down for 37 hours after a billing downgrade and restoration steps.
A Supabase issue reports logical backup commands from PostgreSQL 17.6+ failing when restored to PostgreSQL 15.8.

recurrence: A recent outage report and a concrete backup-version incompatibility show that possessing an export does not prove a recoverable service.
current_workaround: Download a dump, assume it works, test restore only during an incident, or manually inspect SQL headers and extensions.
incumbents_and_gap: Managed providers create backups and pg_restore executes them; neither supplies a small recurring compatibility drill with a machine-readable receipt and known version/extension mismatch explanation.
smallest_useful_product: A local/container CLI that restores a selected sanitized or full backup into an explicit disposable Postgres version, checks extensions/roles/schema readiness, times the run, and writes a signed receipt. Non-goals: backup storage, production restore, or database hosting.
success_measure: A weekly pilot catches an intentionally introduced version or extension incompatibility before a recovery event and produces a pass/fail receipt in under 20 minutes.
monetization: one-time — a local recovery-control utility suits teams avoiding additional data-hosting vendors.
constraints: Use disposable isolated containers; encryption at rest for any saved dump; never run against production connection strings; account for provider backup terms and large-data cost.
why_distinct: It proves restore compatibility on a schedule rather than offering another backup destination or migration framework.

title: Alert Config Ledger
user: Platform teams with alert routes and notification policies spread between dashboards and git who need to answer what changed, where it came from, and whether the live state matches review.

evidence.quote_or_summary: An Ask HN network operator calls documentation a scavenger hunt because distributed source-of-truth systems drift.
Grafana's 125-reaction GitSync request covers alerting contact points, notification policies, and time intervals.

recurrence: Source-of-truth drift is directly reported on HN, while strong demand for Git-synced alerting config shows alert policies are especially hard to audit.
current_workaround: Export dashboard JSON, browse UI history, keep partial YAML in a repository, and reconcile changes during incidents.
incumbents_and_gap: Grafana provisioning/Git Sync and IaC tools manage configurations; a vendor-neutral live-versus-reviewed ledger focused on alert routes and escalation impact is still absent.
smallest_useful_product: A CLI that snapshots configured alert objects through read-only APIs or exports, normalizes them, compares to a git baseline, and renders a timeline of route/recipient/severity changes. Non-goals: sending alerts, replacing Grafana, or configuration writes.
success_measure: In a pilot, every changed alert route is attributed to a source within five minutes and live/baseline drift is detected before the next on-call handoff.
monetization: freemium — basic normalizers should be open, while enterprise adapters and approval reports may justify payment.
constraints: Read-only credentials; redact recipient contact data in reports; source adapters must preserve provider semantics and timestamps.
why_distinct: It is an accountability lens for live alert configuration, not another observability dashboard or IaC engine.

title: Worktree Verifier
user: Developers using multiple agent or human worktrees who need inexpensive continuous smoke validation of each changed worktree without opening a test UI or mixing branches.

evidence.quote_or_summary: An Ask HN user says agent-orchestrator worktree syncing is unreliable and makes local testing difficult.
An 89-reaction Playwright request asks for unobtrusive continuous background validation when test sources change.

recurrence: Agent worktree testing friction is current, and long-standing demand for non-UI continuous validation supplies the complementary workflow signal.
current_workaround: Switch branches, wait for CI, run tests manually in a root worktree, or keep several terminals with unclear test freshness.
incumbents_and_gap: Playwright watch/UI modes and CI run tests, while git worktrees isolate changes. They do not maintain a compact per-worktree status board with explicit freshness, changed-file scope, and bounded smoke commands.
smallest_useful_product: A local daemon/CLI that discovers configured git worktrees, watches relevant changes, runs declared fast checks in isolated worktrees, and serves a localhost status page with last-pass commit hashes. Non-goals: cloud CI, agent orchestration, test generation, or full-suite scheduling.
success_measure: For a pilot repository with three worktrees, 90% of edits receive a relevant smoke result within two minutes and no result is attributed to the wrong worktree.
monetization: free — a local developer utility needs zero-account adoption; paid team observability is optional later.
constraints: Commands must be opt-in and sandboxable; avoid concurrent writes to shared build caches; never expose source or test output off localhost by default.
why_distinct: It coordinates test freshness across real worktrees rather than creating another test runner or AI coding agent.
